content: In the early 1990s, Mexico demonstrated clear evidence of entering a transitional phase in the health status of its population. When compared to the 1940s or even the 1970s, mortality patterns in Mexico during the 1990s more closely resembled those observed in developed nations. The healthcare system in Mexico is generally of excellent quality, and in many areas, it is exceptionally good. A significant number of healthcare professionals in Mexico, including doctors and dentists, receive their training in Western countries such as the United States. Additionally, some American physicians undergo training in Mexico, particularly in Guadalajara. Medium-sized and large cities in Mexico typically have at least one high-quality hospital. One notable advantage of healthcare in Mexico is its affordability. Medical costs are generally lower than what one might expect to pay in the United States. This cost advantage extends to prescription medications as well. Prescription drugs manufactured in Mexico are, on average, about 50% less expensive than similar drugs produced in the United States. During the period of conquest, new diseases were introduced to the indigenous populations, leading to widespread epidemics. Diseases such as smallpox, cholera, typhus, and measles caused significant mortality for centuries. In more recent times, health epidemics have been influenced by urbanization and advancements in transportation. The socioeconomic divide between the upper and lower classes has become evident in the health disparities observed in the Mexican population. On one end of the spectrum, obesity is a growing concern, while on the other, malnutrition and starvation persist, driven by economic stagnation and financial crises. Certain health risks are more prominent in Mexico due to cultural and lifestyle factors. For example, the use of pesticides has become a significant health concern, particularly in states like Chiapas, where 58% of the population is engaged in agricultural work. Despite awareness of safety precautions, public concern about the long-term health effects of pesticide exposure remains insufficient. Many agricultural workers in Chiapas believe that only the weak are affected by pesticide exposure, reflecting cultural beliefs that influence health perceptions and behaviors. Another major health issue in Mexico is the rising prevalence of AIDS (known as SIDA in Spanish). In 1988, AIDS was the 11th leading cause of death in Mexico, but by 1996, it had become the third leading cause of mortality, accounting for 12% of all deaths in the country. Advances in medicine and increased health knowledge have contributed to a 25-year increase in life expectancy during the second half of the 20th century. While the overall health of Mexicans has improved over the past four generations, millions of citizens still lack regular access to healthcare services. The healthcare system in Mexico is structured into three main components: the social security institute, governmental services for the uninsured, and the private sector, which is almost entirely funded out-of-pocket. Governmental services include free healthcare in rural areas provided by the Secretariat of Health, as well as family planning, vaccinations, oral rehydration, and emergency services available nationwide. Between 1985 and 1995, the number of public hospitals in Mexico increased by 41%. However, private hospitals, which require payment, often struggle to provide adequate healthcare. Most private hospitals are small, with 83% of clinics having fewer than 14 beds, and half of those having fewer than 5 beds. Despite the growth in public hospitals and alternative health services, 11% of Mexico's population still lacks access to healthcare services. Financial barriers are a significant limitation, as the cost of medications and treatments can be prohibitively high. Many individuals cannot afford to take time off work, as even a single day of lost income can jeopardize a household's financial stability. Geographical barriers also exist, particularly for rural areas that are far from cities and lack adequate transportation. Organizational barriers, such as a lack of trust or perceived poor service quality, further prevent some individuals from accessing healthcare. These barriers can result in unmet medical needs, particularly in areas such as prenatal care, childbirth, acute diseases, and injuries. Approximately half of Mexico's population is uninsured, and many pay healthcare costs out-of-pocket. For some families, more than one-third of their income is spent on medical expenses. Addressing these disparities requires a healthcare system that accommodates the needs of a divided population, ensuring greater access to healthcare services for the lower-income majority. Health inequities are particularly pronounced among indigenous communities. For instance, 40% of indigenous women are anemic, compared to the national average of 26%. Studies also reveal that in low-income areas, fewer than 10% of pregnant women deliver their babies in hospitals. A restructured healthcare system is necessary to bridge the gap between the upper and lower classes, providing equitable access to healthcare for all.
